q7.answer: The shared state is in Redis, with one set of four keys per document (presence, leases, cursors, presence_ver), and each entry is per connection (connId), not per user. Each node's heartbeat runs a Lua script every 10 s that moves that connection's lease 30 s ahead on Redis TIME and sets the keys to expire in 120 s, so the lease is what keeps an entry fresh.

q8.answer: No node runs cleanup on its own when it dies. The leases stop being refreshed and expire within 30 s, and then a surviving node's sweep (every 10 s, on each node with a local socket on the document) runs a Lua script that removes the expired connIds from presence and cursors. If that was the user's last connection, the script raises presence_ver and publishes leave, and every node forwards that leave to its local browsers, so removal happens within about 40 s.

q9.answer: The sender's node rate-checks the update in memory, then runs a Lua script that stores the cursor in Redis (only if the connId still has a lease) and publishes it on cursor:doc. Each node subscribed to cursor:doc, including other nodes and the sender's own node if it has viewers, receives it from that publish and forwards it to its local browsers. A viewer on the sender's own node therefore gets the cursor through the same Redis publish, which the design implies but does not state in words.

q10.answer: The node subscribes to presence:doc and cursor:doc before it reads anything, so no event can fall between the subscription and the snapshot. It then reads presence, stored cursors and presence_ver in one atomic read, sends the snapshot, and only then forwards presence and cursor events to that browser. The browser ignores presence events at or below the snapshot's version and applies later ones in order, and it drops cursors for connIds it does not have in its list.

q11.answer: Every snapshot is followed by hello, and every browser in the document answers hello by sending its current rev and position, whether or not the user is moving. So a newly joined user sees an idle user's caret as soon as that user's answer arrives, and any stored cursor that can be transformed is drawn from the snapshot in the meantime.

q12.answer: Each receiver checks the seq of each cursor against the last seq it showed for that connId, and drops any cursor whose seq is not higher, so an older message cannot move a caret back. A cursor whose rev is above appliedRev is held, and a newer seq from the same connId replaces the held one, so an older position is never drawn after a newer one. Positions are moved with transformPosition, and a reconnect gets a new connId and seq counter, so it is not blocked by the old seq.
